definition: Downplay means to make something seem less important than it really is.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word downplay. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know downplay should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rescuers downplay their own part in the story, insisting anyone with a rope would have done the same.
Understate is milder than downplay — an understatement may simply be modest or accidental, with no agenda behind it.
Whitewash goes further than downplay: downplaying shrinks a problem that stays visible, while whitewashing scrubs the wrongdoing out of the record altogether.

Minimize is the plain word for treating something as smaller than it is — the fact stays on the table, shrunk. Downplay does the same shrinking but hints at motive: a company downplays a defect because it wants the story small. Minimize describes the act; downplay adds the agenda.

Soft-pedal borrows the piano's quiet pedal: you present a fact gently so it draws little attention, easing past it in a soothing tone. Downplay pushes harder in the same direction, actively arguing the thing is less important than it really is rather than just handling it quietly.
to push something forward as more important than it is
to describe as bigger than the facts allow

When the inspection found rot in the ferry's hull, the operator downplayed the report — 'routine wear,' he told the paper, 'nothing the summer schedule can't survive.' The harbormaster read the same pages and grounded the boat by noon.
Downplay sits between innocent understatement and outright denial: the fact is admitted, but its importance is talked down.
The operator never claimed the rot wasn't there — he worked to make it sound small.
That intent to shrink is what downplay names.
Downplay is the reporter's word for shrinking-without-denying, and it hints at motive.
Understate can be innocent or even admirable; minimize is the plainer synonym; whitewash accuses someone of erasing the fault entirely.

Two days before the state final, Marisol landed badly at practice and felt her ankle give.
At the trainer's table she called it 'a little stiffness,' laced the boot tighter, and jogged in place to prove the point.
Her coach had seen her downplay injuries before; a girl who wants to start in the final needs the problem to look small.
So he asked the question sideways -- had she iced it at home?
-- and watched her wince as she pivoted to answer.
The X-ray that evening found the hairline crack, and Marisol watched the final from the bench, boot propped on the rail.
